lessons.title: Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia
body: Some of the earliest surviving medical writing comes from Egypt and Mesopotamia. In both societies, healing blended practical treatment with religious explanation, and historians warn against separating the two too sharply, since ancient people did not draw our line between medicine and magic.

Egyptian medical papyri survive in copies from the second millennium BCE. The Edwin Smith Papyrus, dated to roughly 1600 BCE and thought to copy older material, is the best known surgical text. It describes a series of cases, mostly injuries to the head, neck and chest, in a consistent format: title, examination, diagnosis, and then a verdict that the case is one the physician can treat, can contend with, or should not treat. Its authors note observations such as a pulsating wound and describe the brain's surface. The Ebers Papyrus, dated to around 1550 BCE, is a much larger collection of remedies and incantations that mentions drugs, skin diseases, eye problems and heart and vessel concepts. Egyptian mummification gave embalmers practical knowledge of organs, but it did not produce a systematic anatomy of the living body.

In Mesopotamia, medical texts are written in cuneiform on clay tablets. Two kinds of healer are usually distinguished. The asu worked with drugs, bandages and simple procedures, while the ashipu, closer to an exorcist, sought a supernatural cause for the illness and used rituals. The two roles overlapped in practice, and a patient might see both. A large diagnostic handbook, traditionally attributed to the scholar Esagil-kin-apli in the eleventh century BCE, organizes signs and prognoses. The Code of Hammurabi, from about the eighteenth century BCE, sets out fees and penalties for surgeons, including harsh punishments for failed operations, which shows that medical outcomes were already a legal matter.

A worked example of interpretation: when the Smith Papyrus tells a physician not to treat a certain skull injury, historians read this less as despair than as early prognosis, a skill that is later central in Greek medicine. A common mistake is to call this period purely superstitious. It contained careful observation alongside ritual, and the texts reveal an interest in classifying cases.

lessons.title: Greece and Rome: Hippocrates and Galen
body: Greek physicians of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE promoted the idea that diseases have natural causes and can be studied by observation. The Hippocratic Corpus, a collection of some sixty texts, is linked to the island of Cos and the physician Hippocrates, though scholars think many different authors wrote it and cannot say which works, if any, are by Hippocrates himself. A key text on the so-called sacred disease, probably epilepsy, argues that it is no more divine than any other disease and arises from natural causes in the brain. The Corpus values careful case histories, prognosis and the importance of diet, climate and regimen.

Humoral theory held that the body contains four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Health was a balance, and illness an imbalance, so treatments aimed to restore it by diet, rest, purging or bloodletting. The theory is wrong by modern science, but it gave physicians a coherent framework and a reason to individualize treatment. The Hippocratic Oath, whose origin and date are uncertain, expresses ideals such as helping the sick, avoiding harm and keeping confidences. The oath in its ancient form includes prohibitions, such as on giving abortifacients, that many modern versions omit.

Galen of Pergamon (born 129 CE) trained in the Greek East, served as physician to gladiators and later worked in Rome, where he attended emperors including Marcus Aurelius. He wrote voluminously on anatomy, physiology and drugs. Roman law and custom restricted dissection of human bodies, so Galen dissected animals such as pigs and monkeys and applied the findings to humans, which led to errors. For example, he described a rete mirabile at the base of the brain that exists in some animals but not in humans, and he believed that blood passed through pores in the septum of the heart. Galen also emphasized experiments, such as tying nerves in living animals to show their functions.

Galen's authority, preserved and extended by Arabic and then Latin translators, dominated medical teaching for well over a thousand years. This is an important lesson: a brilliant system can become an obstacle when it is treated as final. A common error is to say Galen did human dissections. He may have seen human bones and observed wounds, but his anatomy was largely animal.

lessons.title: The Islamic Golden Age
body: From roughly the eighth to the thirteenth century, scholars writing in Arabic, working in cities from Baghdad to Cairo and Cordoba, preserved, criticized and extended Greek and other learning. Translators, among them Hunayn ibn Ishaq, rendered Galen and Hippocrates into Arabic. This was not just transmission. Scholars compared texts with observation and sometimes disagreed with their authorities.

Al-Razi (Rhazes, about 854 to 925) was a physician in Rayy and Baghdad. His treatise on smallpox and measles is often called the first clear clinical distinction between the two diseases, describing the signs of each and their prognosis. His large encyclopedia, known in Latin as the Liber Continens, collected cases and quotations, and he wrote critically of Galen. Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980 to 1037) wrote the Canon of Medicine, a systematic and comprehensive encyclopedia that organized medicine into principles, simple drugs, diseases by organ system and compounded remedies. It discussed ideas such as contagion by invisible agents and the testing of drugs, and was translated into Latin in the twelfth century and used as a standard text in European universities for centuries.

Other important figures include Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (Albucasis) of Cordoba, whose surgical text with illustrations of instruments circulated widely, and Ibn al-Nafis, who in the thirteenth century wrote that blood passes from the right side of the heart to the lungs and then to the left, rejecting Galen's pores in the septum. Historians have debated how widely his idea was known in Europe.

Hospitals called bimaristans, from a Persian word meaning place of the sick, developed in this period. The larger ones had separate wards, physicians, pharmacies and teaching, and offered care to people regardless of wealth in many cases, supported by charitable endowments known as waqf. They were the forerunners of the teaching hospital.

A caution: popular accounts often credit this period with inventing modern science. A better view is that it was a major, creative stage in a long chain in which Greek, Indian, Persian and Arabic ideas were combined.

lessons.title: Medieval Europe, the Black Death and Vesalius
body: In medieval Europe, medical learning revived through the schools and universities. Salerno in southern Italy was an early center, and by the thirteenth century universities such as Bologna, Paris and Montpellier taught medicine from Greek and Arabic texts translated into Latin, mostly Galen and Avicenna. Teaching was text-based: professors read and commented on authorities while barbers and surgeons, who were trained as craftsmen, did the cutting. Monasteries and, later, hospitals provided care and charity.

The Black Death arrived in Europe around 1347 and killed a large fraction of the population within a few years; estimates for the death toll are uncertain, and a rough range of a third to a half of Europe is often cited. Modern genetic studies of ancient DNA indicate that the cause was the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Contemporary explanations included the humors, corrupted air (miasma), astrological conjunctions and divine anger. Even without the germ theory, communities discovered that isolation helped. In 1377, the Adriatic port of Ragusa required travelers from plague areas to wait thirty days before entering, and later Venice used forty days, which gave us the word quarantine, from the Italian for forty.

In the sixteenth century, anatomy was transformed. Andreas Vesalius, a Flemish anatomist at Padua, published De humani corporis fabrica in 1543, with detailed illustrations by artists in the circle of Titian's workshop, based on his own dissections of human bodies. He pointed out many errors in Galen, including that the human breastbone has a different structure than the one Galen described and that the heart's septum has no visible pores. He did so with respect, but it was a landmark in moving from authority to observation. The French army surgeon Ambroise Paré also changed practice in the 1500s by using ligatures to tie blood vessels after amputation instead of boiling oil or cautery.
A worked contrast: before Vesalius, a professor might read from Galen while a barber pointed at an animal part. After him, the student was expected to see the human body directly.

lessons.title: The Scientific Revolution in Medicine
body: In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, medicine gradually shifted from authority toward experiment and measurement. William Harvey, an English physician, published De Motu Cordis in 1628. By measuring the amount of blood the heart pumps per beat and multiplying by the heart rate, he argued that the quantity was too large to be made fresh and consumed by the body, so the blood must move in a circuit. He also demonstrated that valves in veins direct flow toward the heart. Harvey could not see the connections between arteries and veins. Marcello Malpighi, using a microscope in 1661, observed capillaries in the frog lung, which completed the picture.

The microscope opened a new world. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant who ground his own lenses, described bacteria, red blood cells and sperm in the 1670s and 1680s, although no one yet connected microbes to disease. Thomas Sydenham in England stressed careful bedside observation and the natural history of diseases, and is often called the English Hippocrates.

A second line of progress concerned the link between symptoms and the structures seen after death. In 1761 the Italian anatomist Giovanni Battista Morgagni published De Sedibus et Causis Morborum, correlating clinical histories with autopsy findings in hundreds of cases. This is the foundation of pathological anatomy: disease has a seat in organs. In the early nineteenth century, Rene Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816 to listen to the chest and correlated sounds with findings at autopsy.

Another milestone was James Lind's comparison of treatments for scurvy aboard a British ship in 1747. He divided twelve sailors with scurvy into pairs and gave each pair a different remedy, and the pair given oranges and lemons recovered fastest. The trial was small and the Navy did not adopt citrus juice systematically for decades, which shows how slowly evidence changed policy. Vitamin C was identified in the twentieth century.

A worked lesson: Harvey's argument used quantity, not a seen structure, to defeat a theory held for fifteen centuries, and it was strengthened later by the microscope. Good evidence can arrive in different forms.

lessons.title: Germ Theory: Snow, Semmelweis, Pasteur, Koch and Lister
body: Until the nineteenth century, many doctors believed that disease came from miasma, foul air from decaying matter. Several investigators challenged this by observing patterns of illness. John Snow, a London physician, mapped cholera deaths in the Soho outbreak of 1854 and traced them to the Broad Street water pump, arguing that cholera spread through contaminated water. The handle of the pump was removed, although the outbreak was already declining, so the episode is better seen as a method of analysis than a dramatic cure.

Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian obstetrician at the Vienna General Hospital, noticed in 1847 that women died of puerperal fever, a childbirth infection, far more often in the clinic staffed by doctors and students than in the one staffed by midwives. When a colleague died after a cut during an autopsy, with symptoms like those of the women, Semmelweis concluded that the doctors carried something from the dissecting room on their hands. He required handwashing with a chlorinated lime solution, and mortality fell sharply. Many colleagues resisted, partly because the idea implied that doctors had been causing deaths and because he had no theory of a germ. He died in 1865.

Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, showed through experiments with swan-necked flasks that microbes arise from other microbes in the air and not from spontaneous generation, and linked fermentation to living organisms. His work supported the germ theory of disease. Robert Koch, a German physician, demonstrated in 1876 that a specific bacterium causes anthrax, identified the tuberculosis bacillus in 1882 and the cholera bacterium in 1883. Koch's postulates, a set of criteria for linking a microbe to a disease, require that the organism be found in cases, grown in pure culture, cause disease when introduced into a healthy host, and be recovered again. They are a guide with known limits, since some microbes cannot be cultured and carriers exist.

Joseph Lister, a Scottish surgeon, read Pasteur's work and in 1867 began using carbolic acid on wounds and instruments to prevent infection, reporting a sharp fall in deaths. Later surgeons moved from antisepsis, killing germs on contact, to asepsis, preventing them from entering through sterilized instruments, gowns and gloves.

A common error is to say Semmelweis was simply ignored because he was wrong. The better explanation is that he had strong data but no mechanism and a confrontational style, and his message threatened professional identity.

lessons.title: Anesthesia and the Transformation of Surgery
body: Before anesthesia, surgery was a race against pain and shock. Surgeons were prized for speed, and many operations were limited to amputations, stone removal and treatment of injuries. Pain control used alcohol, opium, restraints and assistants.

Nitrous oxide was shown to relieve pain in the early 1800s, but it was not widely used in surgery at first. Crawford Long, a Georgia physician, used ether for an operation in 1842, though he did not publish his work until later. The public demonstration that changed practice happened on October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. A dentist, William Morton, administered ether to a patient while the surgeon John Collins Warren removed a neck tumor. The news spread rapidly across the Atlantic. In 1847 James Young Simpson in Edinburgh introduced chloroform, which was easier to give but carried a greater risk of sudden death from heart effects. John Snow in London made anesthesia safer by studying doses and inhalers, and he gave chloroform to Queen Victoria for childbirth in 1853.

Anesthesia made longer, more careful operations possible, but surgery remained dangerous because of infection. Only when antisepsis and asepsis were combined with anesthesia did the operating room become safer. William Halsted at Johns Hopkins promoted rubber gloves in the 1890s, and surgeons began to explore the abdomen, chest and brain. Blood group discovery by Karl Landsteiner in 1901 led to safer transfusion.

Later milestones include the heart-lung machine, first used successfully for open-heart surgery by John Gibbon in 1953, and organ transplantation. The first successful kidney transplant, between identical twins, was performed by Joseph Murray in Boston in 1954, and the first human heart transplant, by Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town in 1967. Immunosuppressive drugs later made transplants between unrelated people practical.
A useful point: anesthesia did not by itself reduce death rates at first, since longer operations led to more infection. Progress needed several advances working together.

lessons.title: Vaccination from Jenner to Polio
body: Smallpox killed a large share of its victims and scarred many survivors. Long before vaccines, people in Asia, Africa and the Middle East practiced variolation, deliberately infecting a healthy person with material from smallpox pustules to cause a milder illness and later immunity. It carried a real risk of death and could spread the disease. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had seen it in the Ottoman Empire, promoted it in England around 1721, and in Boston Zabdiel Boylston inoculated people during the epidemic of that year on the urging of Cotton Mather.

Edward Jenner, an English country physician, took a different path. Having heard the observation that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed protected against smallpox, he inoculated a boy, James Phipps, with cowpox material in 1796 and later exposed him to smallpox without disease. Jenner published his results in 1798. The word vaccine comes from the Latin for cow. Vaccination was safer than variolation, and spread widely. In the nineteenth century Pasteur extended the term to protection against other diseases and developed a rabies vaccine, first used in a boy named Joseph Meister in 1885.

Smallpox vaccination led to one of the great achievements of public health. A global campaign led by the World Health Organization, using surveillance and ring vaccination, ended with the last natural case in 1977 in Somalia, and the world was declared free of smallpox in 1980. It remains the only human disease eradicated.

Polio, a viral disease that can cause paralysis, caused summer epidemics in the twentieth century. Jonas Salk's inactivated vaccine, given by injection, was declared safe and effective after a large field trial in 1955. That year, vaccine produced by one manufacturer, Cutter Laboratories, contained live virus and caused cases of polio, a reminder that manufacturing control is vital. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine, using weakened live virus, was licensed in the United States in 1961 and was cheap and easy to give. Wild polio has been eliminated from most of the world but, as of this writing, continues in a few countries, and rare cases linked to the oral vaccine's weakened virus are a reason many countries now use the inactivated vaccine.
A worked contrast: variolation used the real disease in a controlled dose, whereas vaccination used a related, milder agent.

lessons.title: The Antibiotic Revolution
body: Before antibiotics, a scratch, a pneumonia or a childbirth infection could kill. The first targeted antimicrobial chemicals came from the German laboratory of Paul Ehrlich, who sought a magic bullet that would attack a microbe without harming the patient. His team's compound arsphenamine, marketed as Salvarsan in 1910, treated syphilis. It was toxic and hard to give, but it showed that chemistry could target an infection.

In 1935 Gerhard Domagk, working at the German company Bayer, showed that the dye Prontosil protected mice and people from streptococcal infection. French researchers soon showed that the active part was sulfanilamide, so a family of sulfonamide drugs followed. Domagk received the Nobel Prize in 1939, though the Nazi government prevented him from accepting it at the time. In 1937 a sulfanilamide preparation made with the solvent diethylene glycol in the United States poisoned more than a hundred people, which led to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938.

Alexander Fleming, at St Mary's Hospital in London, noticed in 1928 that a mold, Penicillium, had killed bacteria around it on a culture plate. He published the finding but could not purify the active substance. In Oxford in the late 1930s and early 1940s, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and colleagues, including Norman Heatley, purified penicillin, showed it worked in mice, and treated the first patients in 1941. Wartime effort in the United States and Britain scaled up production, and by 1944 there was enough for Allied troops. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Selman Waksman, a soil microbiologist, led the team that discovered streptomycin in 1943, the first effective drug for tuberculosis, and he is credited with popularizing the word antibiotic for substances made by microbes that inhibit others. Many other classes followed in the 1940s to 1960s.

Resistance appeared quickly. Bacteria that survive a drug multiply, and resistance genes can spread between species. Fleming himself warned in his Nobel lecture that underdosing could select resistant microbes. The long-term lesson is that antibiotics are a shared resource: overuse in people and animals favors resistant organisms, and the pipeline of new drug classes has been thin since the late twentieth century.

lessons.title: The Modern Hospital and the Rise of Evidence
body: For most of history the hospital was a place of charity for the poor, and people with means were treated at home. Hospitals were often dangerous because of crowding and infection. Several nineteenth and twentieth century developments produced the institution we know.

Florence Nightingale, an English nurse, led a team to the British military hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War in 1854. She emphasized ventilation, cleanliness and nutrition and gathered statistics, showing that most deaths were from disease and not wounds. She was a skilled statistician and used diagrams to persuade officials, and her work led to reform of army sanitation. In 1860 she founded a nurse training school at St Thomas' Hospital in London, which established nursing as a trained profession.

Medical education also changed. In 1910 Abraham Flexner, an educator commissioned by the Carnegie Foundation, published a report on medical schools in the United States and Canada. It recommended that schools be linked to universities, require laboratory science and clinical training, and meet strict standards. Many weak schools closed. The report raised quality, but it also reduced the number of schools admitting women and Black students, as a later lesson shows.

The intensive care unit has roots in the 1952 polio epidemic in Copenhagen. When patients with paralyzed breathing muscles overwhelmed the hospital, the anesthetist Bjorn Ibsen proposed positive-pressure ventilation by tube, with medical students squeezing bags by hand in shifts, and survival improved markedly. This led to dedicated units with specialized staff and equipment.

The randomized controlled trial reshaped how treatments are judged. The British Medical Research Council's streptomycin trial for tuberculosis, published in 1948, is often described as the first properly randomized clinical trial, with allocation by random numbers concealed from the investigators. Over the following decades, controlled trials became the standard for testing drugs, supporting what came to be called evidence-based medicine in the 1990s. In the United States, Medicare and Medicaid, created in 1965, changed who could pay for hospital care.
A worked point: Nightingale's reforms relied on counting and charting, an early example of using data to change institutions.

lessons.title: Women and Minorities in Medicine
body: The history of medicine includes many people who were kept out of the profession and many who were used in research without a choice. Both stories matter to understanding trust and evidence today.

Women were healers, midwives and nurses for centuries, but formal medical degrees were closed to them. Elizabeth Blackwell graduated from Geneva Medical College in New York in 1849 and is regarded as the first woman in the United States to receive a medical degree in modern times. Elizabeth Garrett Anderson qualified in Britain through the Society of Apothecaries in 1865 and later helped open medicine to women. Rebecca Lee Crumpler graduated from the New England Female Medical College in 1864 and is regarded as the first Black woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. James McCune Smith, who earned his degree in Glasgow in 1837 because American schools refused him, is regarded as the first Black American physician with a medical degree.

Institutional barriers continued into the twentieth century. After the Flexner Report in 1910 and the closing of weaker schools, only two historically Black medical schools in the United States, Howard and Meharry, remained from several that existed. Quotas and exclusion limited many women and Black, Jewish and other applicants for decades.

Exploitation in research was another theme. J. Marion Sims, often called the father of modern gynecology, developed a surgical repair for vesicovaginal fistula in the 1840s by operating repeatedly, without anesthesia, on enslaved women including Anarcha, Lucey and Betsey. Historians and ethicists debate how to weigh his contribution against the fact that these women could not consent. The Tuskegee study, discussed in the bioethics course, is another example.

Gaps in evidence also arose. In 1977 a US Food and Drug Administration guideline recommended excluding women of childbearing potential from early drug trials, in part after the thalidomide disaster. This meant that dosing and side effects were studied mostly in men. The NIH Revitalization Act of 1993 required that women and minorities be included in clinical research funded by NIH unless there is a clear reason.
The lesson: who is allowed to practice and who is studied shape what medicine knows and whom it serves.

lessons.title: Public Health Milestones
body: Much of the increase in human life expectancy over the last two centuries came from public health measures that prevent disease in populations, rather than from treatments for individual patients. The key milestones are worth knowing.

Sanitation. Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report on the sanitary condition of the laboring population of Great Britain linked filth and poor housing to disease and argued for drains, clean water and waste removal. The Public Health Act of 1848 set up a national board of health. After the Great Stink of 1858, when the Thames smelled so badly that Parliament was affected, the engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a large sewer network in London. Cholera outbreaks later declined in cities that treated their water.

Water treatment. Filtration and then chlorination of drinking water in the early twentieth century sharply reduced typhoid and other waterborne diseases. Jersey City, New Jersey, began chlorinating its supply in 1908, among the first large US trials. Community water fluoridation, beginning with Grand Rapids, Michigan, in 1945, reduced tooth decay, and remains debated in some places over consent and risk-benefit, though major health bodies have supported it.

Vaccination and disease control, covered earlier, joined a wider set of measures including pasteurization of milk, food safety rules, vector control and oral rehydration therapy, which uses a simple solution of salts and sugar to treat dehydration from diarrhea and is credited with saving many millions of lives.

Tobacco. In 1950, studies by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill in Britain and by Ernest Wynder and Evarts Graham in the United States linked smoking with lung cancer. The 1964 report of the US Surgeon General concluded that smoking causes lung cancer in men and that it is a health hazard, a landmark use of epidemiology and criteria for causation. Smoking rates fell over decades with taxes, labeling and restrictions.

Other measures include seat belt and motor vehicle safety rules, workplace safety laws and lead removal from gasoline and paint. Public health also faces questions of liberty, as the bioethics course discusses.

A caution: the decline of many infectious diseases began before specific drugs or vaccines, so improved nutrition, housing and sanitation clearly mattered, though historians still debate how to apportion credit.

lessons.title: Pandemics: 1918 Influenza and HIV
body: Pandemics test medicine, governments and societies. Two twentieth century events show different lessons.

The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1919 was caused by an influenza A virus of the H1N1 subtype. It appeared in waves, with a severe second wave in the autumn of 1918, and spread widely as troops and ships moved at the end of the First World War. It is often called the Spanish flu, but the name came from the fact that neutral Spain had a relatively free press that reported on it, and does not show that the disease began there; its origin is uncertain. Estimates of deaths range widely, with figures of roughly fifty million often cited and some estimates much higher or lower, because records were poor. Unusually, many deaths were among healthy young adults. Many deaths involved secondary bacterial pneumonia, and no antibiotics existed. Public health tools were limited to isolation, quarantine, masks, closing of public places and hygiene, and cities that used such measures early and kept them longer tended to fare better in later analyses. The virus itself was not identified until the 1930s, and the 1918 strain's genome was reconstructed from preserved tissue in the early 2000s.

HIV/AIDS emerged into recognition in 1981, when physicians in the United States reported clusters of unusual infections in previously healthy young men. The cause, a retrovirus later named human immunodeficiency virus, was identified in 1983 and 1984 by teams including that of Francoise Barre-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier in France, and that of Robert Gallo in the United States. The early years were marked by fear and stigma, and by activism, in which patient groups pushed for faster drug testing and a voice in research. A first drug, zidovudine, was approved in 1987, and combination antiretroviral therapy, introduced in the mid 1990s, transformed HIV from a usually fatal disease into a manageable chronic infection for people with access to treatment. Prevention tools now include treatment that makes the virus undetectable, and pre-exposure prophylaxis. Access remains unequal across the world.
The common lessons are the value of surveillance, honest communication, preparedness and protection of vulnerable groups, and the danger of stigma, which can drive people away from testing and care.

lessons.title: The Genomic Era
body: Genetics entered medicine slowly. Gregor Mendel described inheritance of traits in peas in 1866, but his work was widely recognized only around 1900. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix structure of DNA, building on X-ray diffraction images by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins's group; the contribution of Franklin has been much discussed in later accounts. Frederick Sanger developed a practical method of DNA sequencing in 1977, and the polymerase chain reaction, developed by Kary Mullis in the 1980s, made it possible to copy small amounts of DNA.

The Human Genome Project, an international effort that began in 1990, produced a working draft announced in 2000 and a finished reference sequence declared complete in 2003. Later work in 2022 reported a complete, gap-free sequence of a human genome. The project cost billions at first, but sequencing costs then fell dramatically, so reading a person's genome is now affordable in many settings.

Genomics has changed medicine in several ways. Single-gene diseases such as cystic fibrosis, whose gene was found in 1989, can be diagnosed and screened. Cancer is increasingly classified by mutations as well as by organ, and targeted drugs followed. Imatinib, approved in 2001 for chronic myeloid leukemia, inhibits the abnormal protein produced by the BCR-ABL gene fusion and is a landmark example of precision treatment. Pharmacogenomics uses genetic variation to predict drug response. Large datasets also reveal polygenic risk, in which many small effects add up, though polygenic scores remain imperfect predictors and perform less well in people from groups that were underrepresented in the studies.

The history also contains a caution. In 1999, Jesse Gelsinger, an eighteen-year-old with a metabolic disorder, died in a gene therapy trial at the University of Pennsylvania after a severe immune reaction to the viral vector. The case led to tighter oversight and attention to conflicts of interest. Gene therapy has since succeeded for several conditions, and gene editing with CRISPR has produced approved treatments.
A recurring lesson: reading the code is not the same as understanding its meaning, and benefits of genomic medicine depend on who is included in the data and who can afford access.

lessons.title: Failures and Reversals That Taught Caution
body: Medicine has repeatedly adopted treatments with confidence and later learned they were wrong. Studying these episodes helps explain why modern medicine insists on controlled evidence.

Bloodletting was a standard treatment for about two thousand years, grounded in humoral theory and supported by clinical impressions, since patients sometimes improved afterward for other reasons. Systematic comparison in the nineteenth century, notably by the French physician Pierre Louis, showed no benefit in pneumonia, and it declined.

Thalidomide, sold from 1957 in Europe and elsewhere as a sedative and a remedy for morning sickness, caused severe birth defects, especially limb malformations, in thousands of children before it was withdrawn in 1961 and 1962. In the United States, the FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey withheld approval, partly because of concerns about the data, and the country was largely spared. The disaster led to the Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962, which required drugs to be shown effective as well as safe and strengthened rules for informed consent in trials.

Frontal lobotomy, a surgery that severs connections in the frontal lobes, was developed by the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz in the 1930s, and he shared the 1949 Nobel Prize for it. It was promoted in the United States by Walter Freeman, who used a transorbital approach. Tens of thousands of patients were operated on, often in institutions with little consent, and many were left with serious harm. Effective drugs and critique ended its use.

Hormone therapy after menopause was widely believed from observational studies to protect against heart disease. The randomized Women's Health Initiative, whose estrogen plus progestin arm was stopped early in 2002, found increased risks of breast cancer, stroke and blood clots without cardiac benefit. The rofecoxib (Vioxx) withdrawal in 2004, after trial evidence of increased heart attacks, is another example of safety signals emerging after wide use.

Reversals also run the other way. For decades, stomach ulcers were blamed on stress and acid. In the 1980s Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed that the bacterium Helicobacter pylori causes ulcers, which they supported by culture and by Marshall's well-known self-experiment, and they received the 2005 Nobel Prize.

Lessons: observational association is not proof of benefit, enthusiasm and authority can outrun evidence, harms may appear only in large or long studies, and sometimes a dismissed idea turns out to be right. Good practice is to demand controlled evidence while staying open to new findings.

questions.prompt: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is best known as an ancient Egyptian text on:
choices: religious spells to protect the dead during their journey to the afterlife
the planting and harvest cycles used by farmers in the Nile Valley
the administration of taxes and the storage of grain in royal granaries
surgical cases, mainly injuries, with examination, diagnosis and prognosis

questions.prompt: In Mesopotamian medicine, the ashipu was most like which kind of healer?
choices: a pharmacist who prepared drugs from plants and minerals only
a midwife who attended only births within the households of the poor
an exorcist who sought a supernatural cause of an illness and used ritual
a surgeon who specialized in the removal of cataracts and the setting of broken bones

questions.prompt: Why do historians caution against calling ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian medicine purely superstitious?
choices: The texts prove the people had discovered that germs cause disease
The texts show careful case classification and prognosis alongside ritual
The texts contain no ritual or religious elements of any kind, only practical remedies
The texts show the use of the microscope to examine blood and tissue

questions.prompt: A papyrus case concludes that the physician should not treat a severe skull injury, even though it describes the wound carefully. A historian would most reasonably interpret this as evidence of:
choices: an early practice of prognosis that distinguished curable from incurable cases
a religious ban on any physician ever touching the head of an injured person in Egypt
a failure by the writers to understand that the wound was serious at all
a legal rule that surgeons who failed to heal would receive no payment

questions.prompt: The Code of Hammurabi sets fees and penalties for surgeons. What does this most clearly show about medicine in ancient Mesopotamia?
choices: Surgery was unknown in that society, and the code was written to forbid anyone from attempting it
Healers were paid only in religious offerings and never in silver or goods
The code required all patients to be treated by ritual specialists exclusively
Medical practice and its outcomes were already subject to law and social expectations

questions.prompt: What were the four humors in humoral theory?
choices: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
Blood, water, fire and earth as the basic elements
Heart, liver, brain and lungs as the principal organs
Heat, cold, dryness and moisture as the basic qualities

questions.prompt: Why did Galen's anatomy contain errors about the human body?
choices: He studied only the skeletons of people who had died long ago
He dissected mainly animals and applied the findings to humans
He refused to make any observation and relied only on religious books
